query: Prior calculations on concentrated alloys examined variations in atomic mass and force constants, temperature-dependent lattice heat transport, or DFT-derived elastic properties coupled to analytical conductivity estimates; some estimates require a Debye temperature. The cited simulations generally represented perfect, defect-free bulk crystals. Experiments below 200 K indicate that lattice and electronic contributions in HfNbTaTiZr can be comparable, while measurements from 300 to 1200 K on a specimen containing 1 wt.% oxygen report total conductivity of 10–17 W/(K m). Available analytical approaches do not capture all relevant atomic-scale complexity in refractory high-entropy alloys, and separate transport studies do not establish a predictive solution for this alloy. Given these constraints, what testable hypothesis could an unspecified new predictive approach make for HfNbTaTiZr without conflating lattice and electronic heat transport? Explain why it should outperform earlier approaches, quantify the expected improvement, define its temperature and sample applicability limits, identify supporting observations from the cited work, and specify decisive comparisons with low- and high-temperature measurements that would falsify it.

generation.hypothesis: A new predictive framework that explicitly incorporates atomic‐scale oxygen-induced defect scattering and high‐order anharmonic phonon interactions in HfNbTaTiZr will decouple lattice and electronic heat transport, yielding lattice thermal conductivity predictions that are 30–40% lower at high temperatures (300–1200 K) than estimates from ideal, defect‐free Debye-based models, while also capturing the comparably mixed contributions below 200 K.
generation.material_initial_state: A single-phase, BCC-structured HfNbTaTiZr high-entropy alloy produced with spark plasma sintering, deliberately containing ~1 wt% oxygen, thus exhibiting realistic point defects and local lattice distortions.
generation.intervention: Application of a multiscale predictive model that integrates classical molecular dynamics with ab initio corrections to include explicit oxygen defect scattering and anharmonic lattice dynamics separately from electronic effects.
generation.conditions: Temperature range from below 200 K up to 1200 K; sample with controlled oxygen contamination (≈1 wt%) and microstructural features typical of powder metallurgy routes.
generation.structural_mediator: Oxygen-induced point defects that locally distort the BCC lattice, modifying phonon dispersion and force-constant distributions, and thereby enhancing phonon scattering.
generation.mechanism: Oxygen defects and inherent chemical disorder induce strong force-constant fluctuations and anharmonic lattice vibrations. This enhanced phonon scattering reduces the lattice heat transport relative to defect-free predictions, while the electronic contribution (estimated separately via carrier transport models and the Wiedemann-Franz law) remains relatively unaffected. The decoupled treatment leads to a temperature-dependent separation where below 200 K the lattice and electronic thermal conductivities become comparable, whereas at higher temperatures the lattice part remains markedly suppressed.
generation.predicted_outcome: At low temperatures (<200 K), the model predicts approximately equal contributions of lattice and electronic thermal conductivity. At high temperatures (300–1200 K), the lattice thermal conductivity is reduced by roughly 30–40% compared to predictions from idealized Debye models, resulting in an overall total thermal conductivity in the range of ~10–17 W/(K·m) that agrees within ±20% of experimental measurements.
generation.baseline: Existing analytical and MD simulation approaches that assume perfect, defect-free crystals and use Debye temperature estimations, which do not capture oxygen-induced defect scattering or high-order anharmonic effects.
generation.boundary: The hypothesis applies to HfNbTaTiZr alloys with oxygen contamination up to ~1 wt%. Results may differ if oxygen levels are substantially higher, or if the alloy exhibits secondary phase formation or more complex microstructures.
generation.uncertainty: This proposal extends insights from direct lattice thermal conductivity separation in concentrated alloys (as in PMC4735586::web::012::thermal_conductivity) and from studies showing significant force-constant and anharmonic effects in disordered HEAs (PMC9726824::web::013::discussion), by explicitly incorporating oxygen contamination effects—a factor not previously modeled in detail.

falsification_experiment.design: Fabricate two series of HfNbTaTiZr samples via spark plasma sintering: one intentionally doped to achieve ~1 wt% oxygen and another with minimal oxygen content. Measure total thermal conductivity in the temperature range from 100 K to 1200 K. Independently determine the electronic conductivity using electrical transport measurements and extract the lattice component via the Wiedemann-Franz law subtraction. Compare the experimentally determined lattice thermal conductivity versus temperature to predictions from the new model.
measurements: Laser flash analysis for thermal diffusivity
Electrical conductivity measurement (e.g., using an Ulvac ZEM-3)
Oxygen concentration via spectroscopy or combustion analysis
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If the decoupled lattice thermal conductivity in oxygen-contaminated samples does not show a reduction of approximately 30–40% relative to defect-free (Debye-based) predictions at high temperatures, or if the total conductivity deviates by more than ±20% from the predicted values across the temperature range, then the hypothesis is falsified.

HfNbTaTiZr high entropy alloy was produced by various methods of powder metallurgy including mechanical alloying, sintering, hot isostatic pressing, spark plasma sintering, and high pressure torsion. The microstructure and mechanical properties of HfNbTaTiZr prepared by various methods were examined. It was found that the main problem in fabrication of HfNbTaTiZr alloy by powder metallurgy is oxygen contamination. Samples prepared by cold isostatic pressing followed by sintering and/or hot isostatic pressing contained oxygen in the concentration range of 0.55 wt %–0.85 wt %. Oxygen contamination of samples prepared by mechanical alloying was even higher, and the oxygen concentration in these samples exceeded 1 wt %. Oxygen incorporated into the HfNbTaTiZr samples caused deterioration of mechanical properties (embrittlement) and prevented formation of a single phase random solid solution. Investigations performed in the present work showed that the most promising powder metallurgy method of production of HfNbTaTiZr alloy was spark plasma sintering of gas atomized powder. The difficulty of modeling phonon linewidths in random alloys comes from the complexity of taking into account the quoted three ingredients, i.e. atomic size, mass, and force-constant fluctuations. A simple analytical model, successfully used in mass disordered alloys, assumes phonon scattering from isolated defects and leads to the expression ΓFWHM = π/2(ℏω)2g(ℏω)〈ϵ2〉, where g(ℏω) is the GVDOS and ϵ represents the sum of all kinds of fluctuations contributions. Using this model, we find that the expected broadening from mass fluctuations in our HEA is negligibly small, at most 0.2 meV. Ascribing the whole observed linewidth to force-constant fluctuations, the global behavior is reproduced quite well along the [ζ00] direction using an average force-constant fluctuation ϵ = 〈ΔFij/Fij〉 ~ 20% (see Fig. 7). However, the agreement does not hold in all directions: the observed anisotropy then calls for more complex models. We therefore turn to the recent theoretical work of Mu et al..
